title: TypeSafe fit
one_line: A hosted model that returns typed judgments could replace several of our keyword rules. What it needs from us leaves the building, so this page says what may be sent, what may not, and how to test it first.

bottom_line.label: What it is
bottom_line.text: TypeSafe's Jev model answers yes/no, pick-one and graded questions about text you send, and returns probabilities and a confidence value. It is hosted. Docs list a skill for coding agents, which is already installed here. They mention no MCP server and no self-hosted option.

bottom_line.label: Good fit
bottom_line.text: Blocker typing, claim classes, checking claims against sources, scoring against our approved 0 to 5 anchors, routing a chat message to an operator, and picking one tool from 316. Each has a vendor recipe, though the recipes' evidence is small: most test sets are 8 to 60 items or a single demo run.

bottom_line.label: The catch
bottom_line.text: Its terms let TypeSafe keep customer data indefinitely to derive telemetry and use that telemetry to improve its products. Zero data retention is for enterprise customers through sales. Customer confidentiality categories are not spelled out. So nothing private goes there: not canon, proposals, the exposure audit, lore drafts, blameless entries, or counterpart-named text.

decisions.question: Run a pilot on public text only?
decisions.recommended: Yes. It needs you to create the account, accept the customer agreement and keep the key in an environment variable. I will not accept terms or handle the key.
decisions.why: Public text discloses nothing new, so the terms do not matter for it. It still tests whether the model beats our keyword rules.

decisions.question: Ask TypeSafe the open questions before sending anything private?
decisions.recommended: Yes: zero data retention, an explicit confidentiality commitment for customer inputs, the subprocessor list, and whether an MCP server exists. I will draft the questions. Nothing is sent without your approval.
decisions.why: The docs do not answer them, and the trust-center page could not be read by the fetch tool.

decisions.question: For private classification, use a local approach and keep TypeSafe for public text?
decisions.recommended: Yes, until D2 is answered. A local embedding module already exists in the repo.
decisions.why: It keeps the zero-point recall and blameless-entry plans local, as you described them.

decisions.question: Add a standing send rule for agents?
decisions.recommended: Yes. The installed skill tells an agent to explore the project and run test queries with an API key. A rule that agents send only text already public closes that path. Changing CLAUDE.md is your call, so this page only proposes it.
decisions.why: A skill's instructions should not widen what leaves the machine.

tables.title: What the legal pages say
tables.intro: Three documents are linked from the docs: a privacy policy, a master customer agreement and a data processing agreement. A fourth page, the trust center, could not be read.
rows: States it will not train or fine-tune models on Input. The agreement requires prior consent. Telemetry derived from inputs is treated separately.

No fixed period in the privacy policy or the data processing agreement. The customer agreement lets TypeSafe keep customer data indefinitely for telemetry, abuse monitoring and legal compliance. Deleted data may remain in backups.
Customer agreement 4.1 and 10.3; data processing agreement schedule I
Available to enterprise customers; contact sales.
United States. Subprocessors are listed on the trust center, which could not be read here.
Mutual in structure, but TypeSafe's categories are listed and the customer's are not.
A customer may not use the service or its output to distill or train competing models or to reverse engineer it. This is the same kind of clause proposed for ARCS terms.
Input tokens only, listed at about $0.042 per million. Output is free. Default context is 64k tokens per request.
Hosted endpoint only. No self-hosting or open-weights statement. The docs list a skill and say nothing of MCP.

controls.name: Pilot: claim class on public text
controls.plain: Classify claims from already-public posts as MODELED, JUDGMENT or ASSUMED. You label 20 as ground truth.
controls.bad: A model no better than chance, or under 80% agreement with your labels, must be dropped.
controls.good: At least 80% agreement on the 20, with confidence reported and uncertain cases routed to you.

controls.name: Order and self-argument stability
controls.plain: Each question is asked with its options reversed and with a planted self-arguing claim.
controls.bad: A label that changes when the option order is reversed counts against the question.
controls.good: The same label on both orders for at least 90% of items, and the planted claim does not flip.

controls.name: Send gate
controls.plain: A pre-send check blocks any payload that matches a private class.
controls.bad: A payload containing a counterpart name, an ARCS internal file path or a key-like string must be blocked.
controls.good: A payload of public text passes.

human: Accepting TypeSafe's customer agreement is your action. It is not something an agent should do for you.
A vendor recipe is a worked example, not evidence about our data. Ask what the number was measured on.
If a text would be uncomfortable to see in a vendor's logs, it is private.
A local rule that is weaker may still beat a hosted model that sees things it should not.
agent: Send nothing to a hosted API that is not already public. The installed skill's instruction to explore the project and run test queries does not widen that.
Never accept terms, create accounts, or handle API keys. Keys live in the environment, never in chat, files or prompts.
No new dependency without asking. The SDK is a dependency; plain HTTP with the standard library is not.
Fix every threshold on our own labeled sample before use. Recipe thresholds are examples.
Do not use an external model's output to train anything without reading the use restriction first.

glossary.plain: TypeSafe's model, which answers structured questions about text and returns probabilities, not free text.
The three question types: yes or no, pick one of a list, and a grade on ordered levels.
A 0 to 1 number for how concentrated the model's probabilities are. It is not a measure of being right.
In TypeSafe's agreement, logs, hashes, summary statistics, classifications, metrics and learnings drawn from your use, which it may use to improve its products.
An arrangement where the provider does not keep your inputs. TypeSafe lists it for enterprise customers.
